summary: A blog article giving five breathing tips for open water swimming, such as learning bilateral breathing, practicing hypoxic breathing over 50 meters, and using techniques like looking to the sky and lifting the head in choppy water. It also stresses that breathing confidence comes from practice, including acclimatizing to cold water and wetsuits, and suggests pool drills that mimic open water conditions. The note is mostly the article body, with repeated site navigation and subscription boilerplate removed.
one_line: A blog guide with five breathing tips and pool drills to help swimmers breathe well in open water races.
key_facts: Open water races require an extra level of effort, with swimmers battling waves, wind, currents, sun, and the flailing arms of a hundred other swimmers.
Bilateral breathing means breathing on both sides, and many swimmers revert to breathing to one side as years pass.
Swimmers may need to breathe to both sides in open water to avoid splashes from nearby swimmers or to avoid inhaling a swell from passing boats.
Hypoxic breathing training involves swimming about 50 meters while breathing every three strokes, then every five, then every seven, and eventually once for the entire 50 meters.
The first 200 meters of any open water race or triathlon is described as always intense, with high adrenaline and few opportunities to breathe.
To handle waves lapping into the mouth, the article advises turning the body further than usual and looking towards the sky without completely turning on your back.
When waves are high, the article advises lifting the head slightly above the water, getting a quick breath, then returning to the stroke.
Hyperventilation can stop even the most confident open water swimmer and force them to tread water or pull out from a race.
Wetsuits can be restricting on the diaphragm, so swimmers should get a feel for breathing with one on in colder temperatures.
If a swimmer finds themselves hyperventilating, the article advises slowing down and breathing every four or five strokes.
For pool training, the article suggests lining up two or three abreast and two deep with friends to simulate choppy open water.
Another pool option is to remove lane lines and drop an empty gallon jug attached to a weight under the flags to use as a buoy for turns.
